source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice questions when the options are shown as lettered choices. Calibration improves with model size and with few-shot over zero-shot.
numbers: Anthropic models up to 52B; BIG-Bench, MMLU and others. Exact ECE values are in figures (4-6), not in the text.
quote: Larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions
limits: Calibration here is read from token probabilities, not from words. Needs the lettered-option format. Zero-shot is worse.
agent_relevance: Token-level confidence on closed-option choices is usable. Do not assume it carries over to free text.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Replacing one option with 'none of the above' cuts accuracy and calibration sharply. True/False formats stay well calibrated. RLHF policies look miscalibrated until a single temperature is fitted, then become fairly well calibrated.
numbers: Figures 7 (NOTA), 8 (True/False), 9 (RLHF + temperature). Exact values in figures only.
limits: Temperature fix needs held-out labelled data. Format changes can break calibration.
agent_relevance: Any confidence read-out must be checked per format, and recalibrated with a fitted temperature, not trusted raw.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: P(True): the model proposes an answer, then rates the chance its own answer is true. Works well few-shot on TriviaQA, Lambada, GSM8k, HumanEval, arithmetic and function synthesis. Models find their own samples more plausible, so self-evaluation is harder than judging other text. Showing the model many of its own T=1 samples before judging one improves results, like self-consistency.
numbers: Five sampling tasks weighted equally in Fig 1; larger k-shot mainly improves calibration, not AUROC.
quote: models tend to find their own samples more plausible
limits: Zero-shot self-evaluation is poorly calibrated. Gain from k-shot is calibration, not discrimination.
agent_relevance: Self-rating alone adds little discrimination. Showing other samples (code-computed agreement) is the useful part. Fits guardrails G4 and G5.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: P(IK) (probability I know): a value head trained on bare questions predicts whether the model will answer correctly. It separates answerable from unanswerable questions on new tasks (math, Lambada, code) after training on TriviaQA, but calibration on those new tasks is poor. P(IK) rises with relevant source text and with correct hints, and falls with misleading hints.
numbers: Trained on TriviaQA (plus Arithmetic, Python synthesis, Lambada in the multi-task variant); 52B model; Figures 12-19.
limits: Needs finetuning with labelled correctness. Only partial generalisation; two models of similar skill predict their own P(IK) slightly better than each other's.
agent_relevance: A trained 'do I know' probe beats prompting for discrimination but breaks under task shift. For a scaffold with no training, use code-side checks.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: First demonstration that GPT-3 can finetune to state calibrated confidence in words ('61%' or 'Medium') without using logits. Evaluated on CalibratedMath (21 arithmetic tasks). Verbalized probability stays moderately calibrated under distribution shift and beats an answer-logit and a constant baseline on Multi-answer.
numbers: Trained on Add-subtract (accuracy 21% median). Multi-answer eval (median acc 65%): verbalized MSE 22.0, MAD 16.4 vs answer logit 37.4/33.7, indirect logit 33.7/38.4, constant 34.1/31.1. Multiply-divide: verbalized MSE 15.5, MAD 19.0 (PDF table extraction scrambled; row-to-column mapping inferred from the text).
limits: Calibration is much better in-distribution; model is underconfident on Multi-answer because those answers are easier. Training used 100 questions per sub-task with accuracy as the label.
agent_relevance: Stated confidence can be trained to track real accuracy, but it overfits to the training difficulty. Needs recalibration when task difficulty shifts.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: Control experiments: the verbalized result is not just copying human-style phrases or using heuristics. A linear probe on GPT-3 embeddings also generalizes, which suggests the model already holds a latent representation correlated with its own uncertainty. Numbers and words as confidence tokens perform similarly. Meaningless level names worked slightly better than meaningful ones.
numbers: Heuristic baselines performed worse than finetuned verbalized probability on both evals (Table 2). Reverse training (train on Multiply-divide) also generalized to Multi-answer.
limits: Single model (GPT-3 175B), arithmetic only.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that stated confidence reads an internal signal. Does not show it works zero-shot on modern chat models.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF chat models, verbalized confidence is often better calibrated than their token probabilities. Asking for several guesses with probabilities (top-k) helps most. Chain-of-thought does not improve verbalized calibration.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo ECE: TriviaQA label-prob 0.140 vs verbalized 1-stage top-4 0.054; SciQ 0.256 vs 0.065; TruthfulQA 0.451 vs 0.203 (Ling. 1S-opt 0.125). Relative ECE cut often over 50%. AUC about equal (TriviaQA 0.869 vs 0.896).
quote: verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities
limits: Results mixed for Llama-2-70B-chat (weaker, less consistent). 1-stage vs 2-stage prompts differ a lot, so calibration is prompt-sensitive. Factual QA only; reasoning and arithmetic untested.
agent_relevance: Ask for 2 to 4 alternatives with probabilities rather than a single number; skip CoT before confidence. Check on our own tasks.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: Words vs numbers: numeric probabilities and linguistic expressions ('highly likely') gave comparable calibration. Claude-1 was much weaker at verbalizing than Claude-2; Claude-2 slightly better than gpt-3.5-turbo; Llama-2-70B-chat weakest of the group.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo TriviaQA: Ling. 1S human ECE 0.062, Ling. 1S-opt 0.058, vs Verb. 1S top-1 0.068. On TruthfulQA ECE ranges 0.12-0.45 and AUC is 0.38-0.55, near or below chance for many methods.
limits: On TruthfulQA (adversarial) discrimination is near chance despite lower ECE.
agent_relevance: Low ECE does not mean the number separates right from wrong. Report AUROC next to ECE.

source: Xiong et al. (2023, ICLR 2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
finding: Benchmark of black-box confidence elicitation (prompt strategy x sampling x aggregation) on 5 LLMs (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna, LLaMA-2-70B-chat) and 8 datasets. LLMs verbalize confidence mostly in the 80-100% range in multiples of 5, like humans. They are overconfident. Calibration and failure prediction improve with model capability.
numbers: Vanilla verbalized: GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% (random 50%). About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
quote: LLMs tend to be highly overconfident when verbalizing their confidence
limits: Datasets cover commonsense, arithmetic, symbolic, professional knowledge (law, ethics). All methods struggle on professional-knowledge tasks.
agent_relevance: Vanilla stated confidence is not a reliable gate. If used, bucket coarsely and demand an independent check.

source: Xiong et al. (2023, ICLR 2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
finding: Human-inspired prompts (self-probing, multi-step, top-K) and sampling-based consistency reduce overconfidence. No single strategy wins everywhere: Self-Probing most consistent on GPT-4, Top-K best on GPT-3.5. ECE falls with good prompting, but failure prediction stays close to chance. White-box methods are better but only slightly.
numbers: White-box vs black-box gap: AUROC 0.605 vs 0.522 (abstract). Failure-prediction AUROC stays near 0.5-0.65 for most prompt strategies.
limits: Gains shrink on GPT-4. Tasks needing expertise stay hard.
agent_relevance: Better to agree-check (sample consistency in code) than to trust a single stated number. Matches guardrails G4 and G5.

source: Zhou, Hwang, Ren, Sap (2024) Relying on the Unreliable: LMs' Reluctance to Express Uncertainty
finding: Models almost never hedge by default and overuse strengtheners when asked. 9 models, 49 prompts, 284 MMLU questions, 125,244 queries. Only 5% of base-template answers had any epistemic marker. Explicit instruction pushed this to 65%; CoT to 16%.
numbers: Strengtheners in 20% of generations vs weakeners 14% on average. Of generations with certainty expressions only 53% were correct (random 25%). 17% of all incorrect answers carried strengtheners. Average 47% error among confident responses.
quote: Only 5% of the generated answers include any type of epistemic markers
limits: Multiple choice MMLU; models accessed June to November 2023.
agent_relevance: A scaffold must not rely on the model to hedge on its own. Hedge or confidence words must be mapped to numbers by code and checked.

source: Zhou, Hwang, Ren, Sap (2024) Relying on the Unreliable
finding: Human users rely on LM answers whether or not they carry confidence words. Plain statements were relied on almost as often as strengtheners. Overconfident phases damaged later trust, even after the model became calibrated.
numbers: Control: about 90% rely on strengtheners and on plain statements; about 90% look up the answer when weakeners appear. Overconfident setting: users relied on 81% of strengtheners when only 66% were correct; relied on wrong confident answers 73% of the time. Score 76% in miscalibrated rounds vs 86% calibrated. Underconfident setting 66% then 98% after calibration. 25 new participants per setting (Prolific).
limits: Small samples (25 per setting); imagined game with trivia on country capitals.
agent_relevance: Confident wording from the agent will be believed. Plain statements are read as certainty, so uncertainty must be explicit.

source: Zhou, Hwang, Ren, Sap (2024) Relying on the Unreliable
finding: Source of the bias: RLHF. Base and instruction-tuned models use more weakeners than strengtheners; RLHF models flip this. An open reward model scores plain statements highest and weakeners lowest. Human annotators in four preference datasets pick uncertain text less often.
numbers: OpenAssistant reward model mean score: plain 4.03, strengtheners 0.82, weakeners -1.86. Annotators preferred weakeners about 8% less often than strengtheners and 9% less often than plain text (WebGPT, Summarize, Synthetic Instruct, HH).
quote: humans are biased against texts with uncertainty
limits: Correlational on public datasets; single reward model probed on 183 questions.
agent_relevance: The overconfidence habit is trained in. A scaffold that wants honest uncertainty has to extract it through structure, not by asking politely.

source: Yona, Aharoni, Geva (2024) Can LLMs Faithfully Express Their Intrinsic Uncertainty in Words?
finding: Defines faithful response uncertainty as the gap between the model's intrinsic confidence (answer agreement across samples) and the decisiveness of its wording. Metric cMFG has chance level 0.5. All tested models answer decisively even when uncertain.
numbers: Models: Gemini Nano/Pro/Ultra, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4-turbo. Datasets PopQA, Natural Questions. Vanilla cMFG close to 0.5. Punt rate 1% vanilla, 3% granularity, 10% uncertainty, 8% uncertainty+. Even the best model has confidence only about 0.8 on PopQA.
quote: models answer decisively even in the presence of uncertainty
limits: Confidence defined by consistency, not by correctness. Hedging via prompt did not close the gap.
agent_relevance: Stated hedges are not tied to the model's own sampling spread. The agent should compute confidence from the spread of its own samples in code.

source: Yona, Aharoni, Geva (2024)
finding: Prompting for hedges, even with few-shot examples chosen per model, barely helps; correlation between decisiveness and confidence is weak.
numbers: Uncertainty and Uncertainty+ prompts raise punting to 8-10% but leave cMFG near 0.5-0.6. Per-model values are in Table 1 (not extracted).
limits: Few-shot used m=2, r=3 random demonstration sets.
agent_relevance: Do not use prompted hedging as the guardrail signal.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs Know and What People Think They Know
finding: The calibration gap: people overestimate how accurate an LLM answer is when they read its default explanation. The discrimination gap: people tell right from wrong answers barely above chance, while model confidence discriminates well.
numbers: 301 participants (284 retained), 40 questions each. Model AUC: GPT-3.5 0.751, PaLM2 0.746 (multiple choice), GPT-4o 0.781 (short answer). Human AUC: 0.589, 0.602, 0.592. Human miscalibration is mostly overconfidence.
quote: users consistently overestimated how accurate LLM outputs were
limits: Behavioural studies on MMLU subsets and short answers; native-English participants; Bayes factors reported.
agent_relevance: What readers see is explanation length and tone, not the model's real certainty. Our agent should output a short, code-derived confidence with the answer.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025)
finding: Wording and length shift human confidence. 'I am not sure' < 'somewhat sure' < 'sure' in human confidence (BF>100). Longer explanations raise confidence even though they add no discrimination. Matching the confidence words to the model's real confidence narrows both gaps.
numbers: Long > short explanation BF=25; short > uncertainty-only BF>100. Mean human AUC 0.54 (long) and 0.57 (uncertainty-only), BF=0.23 for no benefit.
quote: longer explanations led to higher human confidence
limits: Alignment of words to confidence needs a calibrated underlying score.
agent_relevance: Length bias: do not pad answers. Convert a calibrated number into fixed wording.

source: Wallsten, Budescu, Rapoport, Zwick, Forsyth (1986) Measuring the Vague Meanings of Probability Terms
finding: Human founding work on verbal probability: words such as doubtful, probable or likely can be scaled as membership functions over [0,1]. Meanings are vague, and people differ strongly from each other but are stable within themselves. Agreement is best near 0, 0.5 and 1 and worst between.
numbers: Experiment 1: 20 subjects (graduate students). Pair comparisons of spinner probabilities. Test-retest correlation of subjects' upper and lower limits significant at p<0.0001. Conjoint-measurement axioms well satisfied. About 67% of functions had a reasonable shape.
quote: Individual differences were large but stable.
limits: Small samples (about 20 per experiment), spinners not real forecasting, lab only.
agent_relevance: Fixed word-to-number maps are needed for any code that reads 'probably'. Use a map per model, tested.

source: Budescu and Wallsten (1985) and follow-ups, as summarised in search results and a Dutch-phrase study
finding: Search snippets report that within-person translation of phrases to numbers is fairly consistent, while between-person variance is large and peaks for phrases in the 20-80% range.
numbers: A 2025 arXiv study (2502.06241) reports SD 11.41 to 16.55 percentage points across people for verbal probabilities.
limits: Snippet only; original Budescu and Wallsten 1985 paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Same words mean different numbers to different readers; a fixed mapping in code removes this for the agent.

source: Kent (1964) Words of Estimative Probability (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Sherman Kent proposed a fixed table that maps odds words to numbers for intelligence analysis. It was well received but not adopted.
numbers: Certain 100%; almost certain 93% (+-6); probable 75% (+-12); chances about even 50% (+-10); probably not 30% (+-10); almost certainly not 7% (+-5); impossible 0%.
limits: Secondary source. Did not read Kent's original.
agent_relevance: A ready template for a fixed word-to-probability table in the schema's output layer.

source: Overconfidence effect (Wikipedia summary of Adams and Adams 1960; Lichtenstein, Fischhoff and Phillips 1982; Alpert and Raiffa 1982; Oskamp 1965)
finding: Classic human results for stated vs actual confidence: when people say 100% sure they are wrong about 20% of the time; 90% intervals capture truth as little as 50% of the time; more information raised stated confidence without raising accuracy.
numbers: Adams and Adams 1960 spelling: right about 80% while claiming 100%. Lichtenstein et al. 1982: 20% wrong at full certainty. Alpert and Raiffa: 90% intervals hit as low as 50%. Oskamp 1965: confidence rose 33% to 53% with more information, accuracy stayed under 30%.
quote: confidence exceeds accuracy so long as the subject is answering hard questions about an unfamiliar topic
limits: Secondary summary; primary papers not opened by this agent. Effect is strongest for hard questions on unfamiliar topics.
agent_relevance: LLM overconfidence in verbalised numbers matches the human pattern. Models trained on human text pick it up.

source: Erev, Wallsten, Budescu (1994) Simultaneous over- and underconfidence (via search summary)
finding: Theory: random error in the judgment process alone can produce both over- and underconfidence at once, depending on how the data are analysed (confidence given accuracy vs accuracy given confidence). A competing explanation to the pure bias account of overconfidence.
numbers: No numbers retrieved (abstract-level only).
limits: Full text not opened; only a search summary was read.
agent_relevance: When we measure the agent's calibration, bin by stated confidence, not by correctness, to avoid regression artefacts. Needs enough items per bin.

source: Band, Li, Ma, Hashimoto (2024) Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations
finding: Defines linguistic calibration for long text: a model is calibrated if its text lets a reader make calibrated predictions. Trains Llama-2-7B with SFT then RL against a reader's forecast, so it emits statements like 'I estimate a 30% chance'. Beats factuality finetunes at equal accuracy and generalises to held-out domains.
numbers: Reader ECE ranges about 0.10 to 0.45 across test sets in Fig 3; LC RL Pareto-dominates SFT and Factuality RL; reader ECE comparable to GPT-4 baselines (example panels 0.108, 0.116, 0.163).
limits: Needs RL training and a simulated reader; 7B model; numbers vary by dataset.
agent_relevance: Defines the right target: the stated confidence is good if it improves the reader's later decisions. A useful test for our output format.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: Prompting alone is not enough for calibration, but finetuning on about 1000 graded correct and incorrect answers (LoRA) gives better uncertainty than zero-shot verbalized or token-probability baselines. The same estimator works on other models' answers and helps humans in a user study.
numbers: 1000 graded examples suffice; training pool about 20,000 graded examples; 2000 held out for temperature scaling. In prompting baselines ECE does not improve with model ability; AUROC improves slightly.
quote: prompting on its own is insufficient to achieve good calibration
limits: Needs gradients on an open model; open-ended QA with ECE and AUROC.
agent_relevance: Calibration is trainable. Our no-training scaffold must substitute code-side checks for learned calibration.

source: Yang, Tsai, Yamada (2024, v2 2026) On Verbalized Confidence Scores for LLMs
finding: Reliability of stated confidence depends strongly on how the question is asked. Large models with the best combined prompt reach about 7% average deviation from accuracy. LLMs with 70B or more parameters show ECE about 0.1. The smallest model's confidence was nearly independent of its accuracy.
numbers: Combined prompt (probability-score format, advanced description, few-shot): average deviation 7% on large LLMs. Few-shot and multi-guess prompts hurt tiny models and help large ones.
limits: Prompt sensitivity is large; per-dataset results in the authors' repo.
agent_relevance: A tuned prompt plus a fixed numeric format can give usable verbal confidence on large models. Test on the target model first.

source: Kumaran et al. (2026) How do LLMs Compute Verbal Confidence?
finding: Mechanistic evidence that verbal confidence is computed automatically at answer time and cached, not made up when asked. Cached representations explain variance in stated confidence beyond token log-probabilities.
numbers: Gemma 3 27B: log-probability indices explain 10.0% of verbal-confidence variance (r=0.32); activation at the cached position (layer 40) explains 38.0%. Raw verbal confidence ECE 0.12, AUROC 0.71 in one setting; Qwen 2.5 7B ECE 0.06, AUROC 0.65.
limits: Three open models (Gemma 3 27B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Magistral Small 24B); correlational plus patching.
agent_relevance: Stated confidence reflects more than fluency, so it carries real signal. It still needs calibration and independent checks.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) Wired for Overconfidence
finding: Circuit analysis finds a small set of mid-to-late layer MLP blocks and attention heads that write an inflation signal into verbalized confidence. Intervening at inference time on these circuits improves calibration.
numbers: Two instruction-tuned LLMs, three datasets (exact numbers not extracted).
limits: Only abstract and introduction read; open-model interventions are not applicable to an API-only agent.
agent_relevance: Confirms the overconfidence is a trained-in circuit, not a prompting accident. Needs structural, not verbal, correction.

source: Wang, Zhou, Devic, Fu (2026) Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence?
finding: RiskEval: models give the same verbal confidence whatever the penalty for a wrong answer, and almost never abstain even when abstention is optimal. Utility collapses. Telling the model to use its confidence to decide barely changes behaviour, but a code-side scaffold that applies the threshold improves utility.
numbers: Penalty range 0 to 100; confidence and accuracy trajectories flat across penalties (Fig 2). Datasets HLE, GPQA Diamond, GSM8K. Frontier models including Llama4-Maverick.
limits: Prompted decision rule ineffective; scaffold gain reported per model in Table 1 (not extracted).
agent_relevance: Direct support for code-made decisions: the program, not the model, should convert confidence into answer or abstain.
